"I can tell you wrote this yourself"
items.content:
Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project.

It's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams 1 , I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback.

When he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with:

"I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI."

At first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to right 10 pages yourself?

But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like.

Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day.

The reason why we've been pushed to use it?

Apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well.

But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career.

It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it.

In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.

It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?

Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend.

The internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more important. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important.

As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking.

Read the books. Write the papers. Search for answers instead of asking AI. Ask a friend. Ask your mum about the mystery illness you're convinced you're developing and then take her advice and try drinking a glass of water.

Think about what the creators of the content you consume want you to think 2 . Treat the things you consume like the Year 7 English class where you were taught how to identify persuasive techniques. Think about things as much as possible.

Please just don't get the AI do it for you.

On a more positive note,…

items.content:

"Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin.

"Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin.

The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

The team estimates that additional air pollution from the electricity demands of data centers in 2023 resulted in about 650 premature deaths across the United States.

Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas.

The researchers built a modeling framework that captures how the electricity demanded by data centers propagates through the nation’s interconnected power grid. The model also considers how atmospheric conditions impact the formation of air pollution in different regions.

The framework identifies power plants across the country whose emissions increase in response to data center electricity demand. In parts of the Midwest, these emissions combine with atmospheric conditions that favor the formation of fine particulate matter, a pollutant that can cause heart attacks, stroke, and lung disease.

The researchers say these results underscore the importance of considering unintended regional health impacts of data centers, and how the location and operations of these facilities affect public health on a broader scale.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy; and senior author of the study.

Selin is joined on the paper by Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student; as well as others at MIT, the University of California at Irvine, and Yale University. The research appears today in Environmental Research Letters .

The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory  estimated that electricity demands of data centers represented about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and resulted in about 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions.

That proportion has likely increased as new data centers continue to be built at a rapid pace.

Many prior studies estimate impacts using average electricity-grid emissions. Like those studies, the researchers assume data centers draw power to run computing tasks 24/7. Their approach also identifies which generators respond to that additional demand hour by hour, allowing them to trace where the resulting emissions and health impacts occur, Chen explains.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” he says.

items.title: Garage Door Spam
items.content:
In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:

I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.

The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit

The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”

The devices have their own web interface:

When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:

The script runs at night checking for an open door:

The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you."

Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:

After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

items.title: Design for Understandability
items.content:
This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

Is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

The tech industry is quickly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard

So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more important than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test

Now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”

You might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: ‘Losing the battle’: AI hands predators new ways to target children
items.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is handing predators and criminal groups new ways to groom, extort and exploit children, while efforts to protect them are failing to keep pace, senior UN officials warned on Thursday.

“We lost the battle on social media because we were lagging behind, and we are now losing the battle on artificial intelligence because we are still lagging behind,” said  Dr. Najat Maalla M’jid , the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children.

She was speaking during a high-level event in the General Assembly on the risks and opportunities of AI to help end the scourge.

In the past year alone, at least 1.2 million children in 11 countries had their images manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes , UN Deputy Secretary-General  Amina Mohammed told the event at UN Headquarters in New York, citing a  recent study by the UN Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ).

Reports of child sexual abuse material linked to generative AI rose by 1,325 per cent between 2023 and 2024 , according to the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, said Dr. M’jid, noting that most AI-facilitated crimes against children remain unreported and under prosecuted.

Chatbots are being used to gain children’s trust, gather personal information and coerce them into sharing explicit images, she said, while deepfakes made with “nudification” apps are used to humiliate, threaten and exploit them .

Profiling and predictive targeting allow predators, traffickers and criminal groups to reach vulnerable children more easily.

John Trenary who has worked on child exploitation investigations for more than 25 years, said predators have always sought ways of “weaponizing technology to exploit our kids”.

But because AI can scale so efficiently – automate and create wholly synthetic content – its weaponisation is “self-perpetuating”, he warned . As soon as investigators get a handle on one way predators misuse it, “something else comes out”.

Kay Chau of the Tech Coalition – a non-profit alliance focused on child protection – said perpetrators may be using chatbots to facilitate abusive role-play or generate grooming scripts , while agentic AI (systems that can carry out tasks independently) is introducing new risks.

Mariana Rozo-Paz of the Datasphere Initiative recalled working with teenage girls on a digital literacy programme in rural Colombia last year. Asked to draw what the internet looked like, the girls drew a girl named Lucia – their AI agent.

“We talk to Lucia every day,” they told her. “Whenever adults don’t want to answer specific questions, we ask Lucia. She’s always there for us. She has intimate mode, best friend mode.”

“ We would never accept a children’s toy being put on the market without proper safety checks, but AI systems are reaching children without the same scrutiny ,” Ms. Mohammed said. “We cannot leave their safety to the goodwill of technology companies.”

In July, Secretary-General  António Guterres   launched the AI Child Safety Pledge. Its aims include making AI systems certifiably safe before they reach children, and zero tolerance of AI-generated child sexual abuse material.

Voluntary approaches by the tech sector are insufficient, Dr. M’jid said, calling for global standards at the core of AI governance, including mandatory child safety and privacy by design.

AI can also help detect abuse material, identify victims and spot early signs of grooming, added the Deputy Secretary-General.

In a World Childhood Foundation study, a young person in Sweden put it this way: “ The technology is really cool. But you can tell that the people in charge of controlling it cannot keep up .”

“Children should never have to tell us that the adults responsible for their safety cannot keep up,” said the foundation’s Secretary General, Paula Guillet de Monthoux.

“It is our responsibility to prove that we can.”

items.title: Cheap to write, expensive to depend on
items.content:
This cutlery is just right for a picnic. Nobody expects it to still be in the drawer in fifteen years.

In Which of your tests would survive a rewrite? , I looked at how the Rust port of 37signals' Campfire was verified. That article asked whether a rewrite is correct. This one asks a different question: can you depend on it?

Coding agents have made reimplementation cheap. Agents ported Campfire from Rails to Rust in about a day . In the PHP ecosystem alone, I count at least four projects that reimplement Composer in Rust. The README of one of them stated that it was built with a lot of help from two large language models. New test runners, frameworks, and even language runtimes appear at a pace that would have been unthinkable a few years ago.

When I look at such a project, my first question is not whether it is fast, or even whether it is correct. It is whether it will still be maintained in five years, or in fifteen. Composer and Packagist have been around for fifteen years , and I have been maintaining PHPUnit since 2000. Will the rewrite be around that long? And what happens to the projects that depend on it if it is not?

Composer is a good illustration of what it takes for a tool to last. Work on it began in February 2011, and the first commit was pushed in April of that year. Composer 1.0 was released exactly five years after that first commit, by which time it had long become the standard way to manage dependencies in PHP. Composer 2.0 followed in 2020, with a rewritten dependency resolution pipeline.

None of this was a matter of writing code once. Composer has received more than 13,000 commits from over 1,000 contributors. Packagist.org grew from a single personal server into a highly available setup with mirrors around the world. For ten years, Private Packagist, the company the two founders started to make the project sustainable, has covered most of the cost of running both. The team today is just over ten people, and in 2026 much of their work is supply chain security : malware detection, immutable releases, and responding to attacks in the middle of the night.

The interesting part is how Composer started. In July 2011, Jordi Boggiano wrote that the dependency solver still had a bug and that Nils Adermann was the only one who knew that code. In today's terms, Composer had a bus factor of one. That is how most projects start, including the ones that later carry an ecosystem. Being new and having a single maintainer does not disqualify a project. What matters is what happens next: whether other people come to understand the code, whether someone pays for the work, and whether the project makes promises and keeps them.

This is what I mean when I say that writing was never the expensive part. Over its lifetime, a dependency costs far more to maintain than it ever cost to write: bug fixes, security responses, compatibility with new versions of PHP and of everything around it, answering questions, reviewing contributions, keeping a release process trustworthy. Coding agents have made the initial writing dramatically cheaper. They have not made a commitment to do all of the above for fifteen years any cheaper.

The day before this article was published, Daniel Stenberg wrote about two rewrites of curl in Rust , under a heading that could stand above this section: “Writing code once was never the issue”. He counted what happened in curl during the little more than three weeks that agents needed to convert its C code to Rust: more than 300 commits were merged, a little over 200 of them bug fixes that, as he notes, none of the rewrites has. He points to decades of API and ABI stability and writes of an alternative that appears today that it “might be able to do it as well, and in a few decades we will know if they could”.

I do not think that software built quickly, or built by agents, is bad in itself. In 2020, Robin Sloan wrote a lovely essay about a messaging app he built for his family . It has four users, it…

items.title: Pancreatic cancer halted by virus injection in three patients
items.content:
A scanning electron micrograph of pancreatic cancer cells

ANNE WESTON, EM STP, THE FRANCIS CRICK INSTITUTE/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY

A virus has stopped pancreatic cancer in its tracks in three people in a clinical trial in the US. Further evaluation is needed in larger trials, but the early results are encouraging, especially since only small doses of the virus were administered for initial safety testing.

“We only injected one-tenth of the dose we are eventually aiming at, so the efficacy is better than I expected, especially as this is pancreatic cancer,” says Masato Yamamoto at the University of Minnesota, who led the development of the viral treatment.

Woman in cancer remission without treatment in highly unusual case

Pancreatic cancer is notorious for being the deadliest type of the condition. One reason is that symptoms tend to appear late, when the cancer has already spread and cannot be surgically removed. Once diagnosed, people usually live only around three to six months .

Another reason is that pancreatic tumours have tough, fibrous exteriors that block chemotherapy drugs from getting in. “They’re hard as hockey pucks,” says Yamamoto. Immunotherapies that boost immune activity against cancer are also ineffective, because pancreatic tumours can hide from the immune system .

The first patient in the trial, who had a pancreatic tumour 7 centimetres across, was administered the treatment a year ago, and the other two have been since then. At the time, their tumours hadn’t spread beyond the pancreas. Since being treated, their tumours haven’t grown any further. “They are all still alive and have clinically stable disease,” says Yamamoto, who presented the results at the annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy in Boston, Massachusetts, earlier this month. Another 15 patients will now be given higher doses to find the optimum level.

“I think this is an interesting early signal, but as a pancreatic surgeon, I think it’s important to keep perspective,” says Kai Brown at Royal North Shore Hospital in Sydney. “The history of oncology is littered with promising early signals that vanished by the time rigorous phase III [late-stage] testing was done, so I think these preliminary conference results should probably just be seen as hypothesis-generating at this stage.” He also notes that the trial so far hasn’t included a control group, so it is hard to know whether the cancer-killing virus works better than other treatments or none at all.

The virus is an adenovirus that has been genetically engineered to replicate only inside tumours and not healthy tissue. Its replication is specifically activated by an enzyme called cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2), which is present at much higher levels in cancer cells than in normal ones. After cancer cells become infected with the virus, they burst open and die, releasing more virus that can infect neighbouring cancer cells.

In the trial, the virus was injected directly into the patients’ tumours through a thin tube that was guided down a patient’s throat to their pancreas. The tube had an ultrasound probe on the end to allow visualisation of the tumours.

The reason the tumours have stopped growing but haven’t become any smaller may be due to the low treatment dose, says Yamamoto. He thinks they may start to shrink as the virus has more time to replicate.

As the tumour cells start to break apart and leak their contents, the immune system may also be able to recognise and fight the cancer, says Yamamoto. “The patient’s immune system can realise something is wrong, and then go and attack the tumour,” he says. The hope is that the immune system will also recognise and destroy any tumour cells that have spread to other parts of the body. If so, the treatment could be effective against metastatic pancreatic cancer.

items.title: Hackers Leak User Data From JPMorgan, Visa, and Mastercard: It's been a banner week for cyberattacks.
items.content:
The hacks just keep on coming. Days after a major breach of websites belonging to some of the world’s top companies and organizations, data belonging to thousands of credit card users has been leaked by a ransomware group.

According to the Wall Street Journal , the data comes from a blend of customers from Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase, though it was obtained through an exploit of third-party service platforms.

Spokespeople for the companies said the breach encompasses marketing data like names and email addresses, and denied that payment information was obtained as part of the hack. The financial firms also denied that the breach was related to the previous cybersecurity incidents earlier this week.

“There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” as JPMorgan Chase told the WSJ .

The ransomware group n0n claimed responsibility for the breach. According to cybersecurity firm ZeroFox Intelligence , n0n is a hacking collective that often uses a technique known as double extortion, where hackers essentially demand a ransom from victims both to unlock existing files and stop stolen data from being leaked further.

N0n is a new player, with its first appearance coming in September of this year, per ZeroFox. Since then, the collective has conducted an average of two cyberattacks per day, putting it among the cybersecurity firm’s list of “top five most active threat actors globally.”

It’s already been an exhausting week of outages, cyberattacks, and tech disruptions — and if this latest incident is any indication, we’re not out of the woods yet.

items.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
items.content:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here .

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

items.title: We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit
items.content:
Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST

Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:

The drive and determination to force the system to work

Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.

Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365 , Air Traffic Control , United Airlines' systems , the NSA's network , many major banks , Apple's systems , and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

I guess that depends on how you look at it.

I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: The RedMonk Agent Activity Index, Q3 2026
items.content:
Having spent more than a decade seeking to understand developers via the quantitative traces they leave behind in the communities they inhabit and the tools they choose, the time has come to do the same with agents: introducing the first edition of the RedMonk Agent Activity Index.

For over fifteen years, RedMonk has been tracking the relative performance and popularity of programming languages within two datasets: GitHub and Stack Overflow. We replicated a study originally performed by Drew Conway and John Myles White and then repeated it at regular intervals, which offered the ability to not only evaluate a snapshot of a given period, but to monitor shifts and trends within programming language usage over time . The sources for both of the axes for our study have degraded over time, and while it’s not strictly because of agents, they are a major factor.

The monumental impact of coding assist agents has led to a fundamental rethinking of RedMonk’s programming language rankings, which we’ll have more details on within the next few weeks.

While we were looking at the data and attempting to evaluate that impact quantitatively, however, it became apparent that in addition to tracking the relative performance of programming languages that there were some interesting quantitative insights to be found about the agents themselves. As with the language rankings, there are many caveats and much that remains opaque quantitatively about agents, but there is a great deal about agent usage, traction and patterns that can be usefully studied. Their popularity relative to one another; variations in usage amongst specific programming language communities; and even whether they’re permitted to be used at all. And much like the rankings, we’re interested in what the current snapshot tells us, but we’re even more interested to see how this data changes over time.

While we’ve looked at agent activity within specific projects as well as wider communities , this is our first attempt to understand these new New Kingmakers in a broader context.

Before we get into the charts, a few important caveats:

Different agents leave different fingerprints, and some leave none at all. All that we can reliably establish, then, is a usage floor. We cannot measure the ceiling.

Tools that leave footprints will be over-represented in this sample; tools that leave no trace conversely will be under-represented or not counted. As will be unreported coding assistance by humans.

Different version control sites or forges are a challenge to measure relative to one another. First, for obvious sample size considerations, but also because API access and transparency is not consistent from forge to forge. Some could not be queried at all. Several charts in this analysis, therefore, are GitHub-only both because it’s the largest sample but also because its API offers some of the best visibility.

Agent Traction : Across a thirty language sample – the top twenty by PRs and another ten selected for their significance – agents opened 13.9M of 45.4M pull requests on GitHub in Q3, or 30.5%. GitHub’s own figure for September was over 40%, up from 17% in March. There are a few reasons for the disparity: GitHub’s numbers include public and private repos, ours can only survey public. Their figure was for September only, ours was a three month sample, and GitHub has inside access to PR-creation while we’re restricted to public fingerprints. Ultimately, both the findings here and those from GitHub’s Octoverse are consistent with a market in which agent traction is accelerating.

Claude Code Usage : As has already been discussed, the challenges involved in measuring agent traction are many. Some tools are particularly underrepresented, but every agent in this survey likely had some usage uncaptured. There are undoubtedly selection and sample biases potentially in play as well. In StubGenerator::generate_base64_decodeBlock() (x86_64 AVX-512 VBMI path), L_finalBit handles 1-63 leftover bytes with a masked vector sequence that computes output_size = (len/4)*3 . Valid inputs always have a length multiple of 4, so this bug triggers only on invalid inputs: with length < 4 (e.g. "A".repeat(64)+"=" leaves 1 byte after L_process64Loop ), output_size starts at 0 and the padding path decrements it below zero, producing a wrong output_mask . The stub stores past the logical output length before returning to Java, corrupting the heap.

The suggested fix is to early-return to Java if length < 4 .

items.title: Jujutsu Primer
items.content:
This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu ( jj ) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository , so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git .

Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here , but here are a few common methods:

# (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH)

cargo install -- locked -- bin jj jj-cli

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:

jj config set -- user user.name " Some One "

jj config set -- user user.email " someone@example.com "

You can edit jj ’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:

In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:

A commit , also called a revision , is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

@ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 8 49165bc

◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d

The IDs on the left hand side ( royxmykx and kpqxywon ) are change IDs , which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example,

instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon , we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k .

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show , using its short prefix 2 .

Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6ce37c55adba9e8fb

◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Vim without the mystery
items.content:
Vim has a reputation. The most famous joke about it is that nobody knows how to leave: a file opens by accident, the keyboard stops doing what keys normally do, and the only way out seems to be closing the terminal.

All of that confusion comes from one idea that nobody explains at the door. Once it clicks, Vim stops being a puzzle and starts feeling like a small language for talking to text. This post goes from "how do I get out" to editing comfortably, one step at a time. The best way to read it is with a terminal open, running vim practice.txt , trying things along the way. Nothing here can break.

If only one thing sticks, make it this. Press Esc , then type one of these and hit Enter:

:q : quit. Vim refuses if something changed and wasn't saved, which is a feature.

:wq : save and quit. :x and ZZ do the same.

The colon opens a small command line at the bottom of the screen, and whatever is typed there runs on Enter. When everything feels lost, Esc a couple of times always leads back to where it started.

The story starts in 1976, at UC Berkeley. Bill Joy added a full-screen "visual" mode to ex , a line editor, 1 and that mode became vi . He wrote it on a Lear Siegler ADM-3A terminal, and that keyboard explains a lot. It had no separate arrow keys: the arrows were printed on H , J , K and L . And Esc sat where Tab is on today's keyboards, one finger away. Moving with hjkl and pressing Esc all the time made perfect sense on that machine, and the habit stuck.

In 1988 Bram Moolenaar, a Dutch programmer, started writing a vi clone for the Amiga. He called it Vi IMitation. It went public in 1991, and around version 2.0, in 1993, the name became Vi IMproved. Bram looked after Vim for more than thirty years, until he died in 2023. 2 A group of longtime contributors maintains it now, and Vim 9.2 came out in February 2026.

There's also Neovim, a fork started in 2014. Everything in this post works the same way in both.

In most editors, the keyboard always types. Press d and a "d" shows up on the screen.

Vim has modes, and the keyboard means different things in each one:

- Normal mode: where Vim starts, and where most of the time goes. Keys are commands: d deletes, w jumps to the next word, u undoes.

- Insert mode: the keyboard types, like in any other editor. The bottom of the screen says -- INSERT -- .

- Visual mode: select text first, then act on the selection.

- Command-line mode: the : from the way out. It runs longer commands, like saving or search and replace.

The trick is to see Normal mode as home. Insert mode is where text gets typed, and Esc comes back. Editing in Vim is mostly moving around and changing things, and typing new text is a short trip. That's why the "typing" mode isn't the default.

From Normal mode, any of these goes into Insert mode, each starting in a different spot:

a : insert after the cursor (think "append").

I : insert at the beginning of the line.

o : open a new line below and start typing there.

Type the text, press Esc , and it's back home. A is worth trying on any line: it's the fastest way to add something at the end, no matter where the cursor is.

The arrow keys work, and there's no shame in using them at first. These are the moves worth learning next, because they save the most time:

h j k l : left, down, up, right. j looks like an arrow pointing down, if that helps.

b : jump back to the start of the previous word.

^ : go to the first character that isn't a space.

f( : jump forward to the next ( on this line. Works with any character.

Ctrl-d and Ctrl-u : scroll half a page down and up.

Most moves accept a number in front: 3w jumps three words, 5j goes down five lines.

This is the part where Vim starts to make sense. Commands are built like short sentences: a verb, then a place.

c : change (delete, then switch to Insert mode).

Any verb in front of any motion from the last section makes a command:

dgg : delete everything up to the top of the file.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-133652 📢 Source: CIRCL 💣 CVSS Score: 7.2 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Flowintel , contained a session management vulnerability in its browser authentication mechanism. The session identifier used a bare numeric user ID rather than a credential-bound token, resulting in several related weaknesses: - Remembered logins (remember-me cookies) remained valid after a user changed their password, allowing an attacker holding a previously issued cookie to retain access indefinitely. - Server-side session identifiers were not rotated upon login (local, SSO, or remembered), enabling session fixation. - Self-service email and password changes did not require verification of the current password, permitting an attacker with an active session to modify account credentials without knowledge of the existing password. - Administrator-initiated password resets did not revoke other browser sessions, invalidate remembered logins, or rotate the affected user's API key. An attacker who obtained a valid session or remember-me cookie (e.g., through XSS, network interception, or cookie theft) could maintain unauthorized access even after the legitimate user changed their password. Additionally, an attacker with any valid session could change the account's email address or password without knowing the current credentials, effectively taking over the account. Mutex poisoning is not for everyone
items.content:
After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I

thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment

on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the

language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as

it significantly pessimises code performance in the general case

while encouraging bad code patterns to deal with its weirdness

that doesn’t even solve the general problem.

In theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of

data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then

encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its important work. For example:

fn important ( always_even : Arc < Mutex < i32 >> ) -> i32 {

// Invariant: always_even must always be even

let mut handle = always_even .lock () .unwrap ();

The following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the

always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle

this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a

boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError) , which will trigger a panic

when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

You might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real

cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much

simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid

in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data

that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve

written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this

I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how

you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly

support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she

works on lend themselves more towards these issues compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should

make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

This section is only tangentially related to the topic at hand, but I already wrote it and wasn’t

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up
items.content:
In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”

A screenshot of the top of Amazon’s homepage.

A screenshot of the top of Amazon’s homepage.

I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518 ), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:

Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April . What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

The messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its users.

Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports .

Finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

The Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

Scharon is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica writing news, reviews, and analysis on consumer gadgets and services. She's been reporting on technology for over 10 years, with bylines at Tom’s Hardware, Channelnomics, and CRN UK.

items.title: This Week in Kwi: First release!
items.content:
We have just published the first ever Kwi release! Now we can't use the "it's not even a v0.1.0 yet" excuse any longer: It now is, in fact, a v0.1.0!

(If you're just tuning in now, check out our introduction post from a few weeks ago!)

You can also find a classic source archive on KDE's file servers, and this is what you should be using if you're a distro packager.

The usual caveats apply - a v0.1 is still a v0.1, of course, and translation work is just beginning; expect the latter to improve in subsequent releases.

Let's take a look at what else has transpired in the preceding week.

Terminal: Link hover decorations are now always shown; opening a link still requires pressing the Ctrl key, unless you change the setting for this (feedback on Matrix)

Link detection is more robust, avoiding certain false positives ( bug #528844 )

General UI: Support for global menus and the menu button on the window title bar has landed

Tapping Kwi on touchscreens will now open the on-screen keyboard (user request on Matrix)

Tab bar: The much-requested option to hide the tab bar for single tabs has materialized ( work item #6 )

Tab traversal using Ctrl+Tab now follows last-used order instead of just going between the last two active tabs ( feature request #528798 )

The minimum width of tab buttons has been reduced considerably, allowing more tabs to fit before the tab bar scrolls (user request on Matrix)

Kwi no longer forgets to select the last remaining tab when all others have been closed

Theming: It's now possible to select the system color scheme that Kwi windows should use (separately from the terminal color scheme) (popular request)

The background opacity setting is now also applied to the scrollbar, which makes translucent windows a lot more pleasant (feedback on reddit)

Indicating activity on background tabs now uses a color role that works well with more color schemes ( bug #528794 )

Terminal color schemes in the Settings dialog are now sorted alphabetically (the automatic "System" scheme stays at the top of the list)

Keyboard: Scrolling by line using Shift-Up/Down now works ( feature request #528797 )

The keyboard shortcuts for line-wise and page-wise scrolling are now configurable ( bug #528843 )

KPart (embedding into Yakuake, Dolphin, Kate & co): Fixed conflicts with host app keyboard shortcuts in certain situations, which e.g. broke New Tab in Yakuake

Foreground process information is now refreshed immediately when the host app queries for it, which e.g. fixes Dolphin sending directory change commands at inappropriate times

Packaging: Flatpak Nightly packages now identify themselves as Nightly builds in menus, launchers, etc.

Project bits: Kwi has passed KDE Review and is an official KDE project now ( work item #10 )

Size-specific icons are now installed as pre-rasterized PNG instead of SVG

Additionally, because Kwi is built on KDE's latest technologies, we sometimes get to find and fix bugs upstream of the project, or contribute new features needed by Kwi.

Upstream This Week - by Kwi, for everyone:

In Kirigami Application Components we improved the search in the Shortcuts Editor that Kwi and other KDE apps use to allow you to search for key bindings, so you can find an action by the shortcut you know it responds to.

Also in Kirigami Application Components , we fixed invoking actions in the Find Action dialog using the Enter/Return keys ( MR #29 ).

Unfortunately there will be a brief interruption in this newsletter next week due to some travel!

Stay tuned for updates on the projects mentioned last week (a Plasma setting to switch classic KDE apps over to embedding Kwi, and early work on Split Panes) in the weeks thereafter.

California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe

12 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Lily Jamali North America Technology correspondent

California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.

How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

items.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
items.content:
This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" ( CVE-2026-121481 ) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock() : NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int . The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending.

Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() .

I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths.

Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX .

I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod .

Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable ( env:VAR ), otherwise the command line will be too long.

Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840 .
